invalid_failure_risks: npm internet access not guaranteed: if async-mutex is not pre-installed and container is offline, solver must implement own promise-queue mutex, adding environmental uncertainty
80 req/s throughput threshold is hardware-dependent: on a constrained 1-CPU container, even a correct WAL+per-user-lock solution may fall short on slow CI runners, causing flaky failures
Rolling 60-second window algorithm not precisely specified (sliding vs epoch-bucketed tumbling) — different valid implementations produce different acceptance decisions at window boundaries
The '1 ms' consistency tolerance appears only in the test spec, not in the solver-visible instruction — solver cannot know the acceptable error margin

50-concurrent-request 'exactly 1 accepted' assertion is sensitive to async scheduling; a correct per-user mutex should guarantee it but Node.js event loop timing could yield 0 or 2 on an overloaded system
Pre-populated 48-hour historical records in the DB could confuse rolling-window calculations if the implementation does not correctly scope the 60-second window to current time
review.reasons: The task is realistic, clearly specified, and tests multiple interacting bugs that require both code-reading and runtime verification. The genuine_difficulty score of 3 is borderline — bugs are visible in source and ~16 commands likely suffice — but the performance threshold and the two-bug interaction (TOCTOU + Map-vs-DB) create meaningful failure modes that a non-thorough agent will hit. The hardware-dependent throughput threshold and missing npm package pre-installation are the main risks to fix before building.
fixes: Pre-install async-mutex (or equivalent) in the Docker image so the solver is not blocked by missing npm packages in an offline environment; alternatively, document that the solver must implement their own per-user promise queue

Calibrate the 80 req/s threshold against the actual container spec (1 CPU / 2 GB) by running the throughput test on the target hardware before publishing, and lower it if WAL+per-user-lock only achieves ~70 req/s on that hardware

Add the sliding-window algorithm spec to the instruction (e.g., 'uses a sliding window: the sum of cpu_ms for records with ts >= now-60000 must not exceed 500') to eliminate ambiguity and prevent a valid but differently-shaped implementation from failing boundary tests
State the consistency tolerance ('within 1 ms') explicitly in the instruction so solvers know the acceptable error bound for floating-point summation differences
Confirm in the environment spec whether the container has outbound internet access for npm installs, or list all required Node.js packages that are pre-installed
